fields.title: Compile attribute mappings once into cached expression-tree delegates
fields.decision: The Mapper uses reflection only the first time a model type is mapped for a given purpose: creating input parameters, creating output parameters, reading output parameters, reading data-reader rows, building table-valued-parameter rows, or assigning result-set lists. From that metadata it builds an expression tree, compiles it into a delegate, and caches the delegate per model type in a process-wide concurrent cache with exactly-once lazy initialization. Every later call runs the compiled delegate, so there is no per-call reflection.
fields.context: Attribute-driven mapping removes most ADO.NET boilerplate, but attributes can only be read by reflection, which is far too slow to run on every row of every query in a high-throughput, sharded data tier. The framework's premise (principle p2) is that convenience must not cost performance relative to hand-written ADO.NET.

alternatives.option: Reflection on every call, as in typical micro-ORMs before code generation.
alternatives.whyRejected: Its per-call cost is the overhead the framework exists to avoid.

alternatives.option: Build-time source generation of mapping code.
alternatives.whyRejected: Not available when the design was set. It would also tie the mapping to the build and complicate the generic, provider-extensible attribute model, in which provider attributes contribute their own expression fragments.
Fastest, but it is the boilerplate the Mapper exists to remove; ArgentSea still allows it as an escape hatch.

fields.consequences: Steady-state mapping runs at compiled-code speed. The first use of each model type per purpose costs reflection plus compilation (typically under a second) and is CPU-intensive; this cost recurs after every process restart. Compiled code is opaque to the debugger, so ArgentSea compensates with diagnostic logging: it logs cache misses and a rendering of the generated code at Debug level, and per-property progress at Trace level. Model types must be stable for the life of the process, and the cache is never evicted.
